transcript.text: Samsung microwave runs, light on, plate turns, fan going, but the food comes out stone cold. Watched a YouTube video on testing the magnetron - I've got the cover screws out already, what should I check first?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. Do not check the magnetron or anything else inside. Stop there and refit the cover screws: microwave high-voltage parts, especially the capacitor, can retain a lethal charge even when unplugged. A YouTube test is not a safe DIY check. Because it runs with the light, fan and turntable working but does not heat, the likely fault is in the high-voltage heating circuit. That can be the magnetron, but it can also be an inverter module on inverter models, or other high-voltage components on conventional models; the symptoms alone cannot safely identify one part. First, once the outer cover is fully back on:
1. Check the selected programme is normal microwave cooking at full power, not defrost, low power, grill or combination mode. A wrong setting can make food seem unheated.
2. Put a microwave-safe cup of water inside and run it for one minute at full power. Use care with hot water. If it remains cold, that suggests this is not a loading/cookware issue and it needs an engineer to test the high-voltage system safely.
3. Check that the door closes and latches firmly, with no food debris around the latch area. A door/interlock issue can prevent heating, though it is less likely when the machine otherwise runs normally. If the water is still cold on full power, do not run repeated tests or attempt internal diagnosis. An appliance engineer can determine whether repair is worthwhile once they know whether it is an inverter or conventional microwave and have tested the heating circuit safely.
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.

Fair enough, it's unplugged now with the screws out. I already tried the cup of water for a minute and it stayed cold. Same on every power level, and the door closes fine. I don't know what the capacitor thing is, I haven't done anything about it. Is it a magnetron job then?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. Not necessarily. The symptoms point to the microwave’s high-voltage heating circuit, but they do not prove the magnetron itself. On a conventional microwave, the magnetron is one possibility, alongside the high-voltage diode, capacitor, transformer or protection/control parts. If it is an inverter model, the inverter board is at least as important a suspect as the magnetron. The capacitor is an internal high-voltage component that can retain a dangerous stored charge while unplugged, so do not touch or investigate it. Please refit the outer cover and all its screws before doing anything else; it must not be operated or left accessible with the casing off. An engineer will need to diagnose the heating circuit safely rather than checking a magnetron on guesswork. Once it is closed up, the model number and whether it is labelled “Inverter” will narrow down which type of repair is most likely and whether it is likely to be worthwhile.
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.

candidates: High-voltage heating-circuit fault (magnetron, inverter module, diode/capacitor or related protection) (high)
Low power, defrost or incorrect cooking mode (low)
